evidence_quotes.quote: O objetivo deste artigo é analisar alguns aspectos da relação entre população e recursos hídricos. Investiga a percepção cultural e usos locais da água para compreender de que formas tais costumes dialogam ou conflitam com as normas legais e técnicas propostas pelas agências reguladoras do recurso.
Ao todo, no período 1999/2002 foram pesquisadas 22 comunidades e entrevistadas 188 famílias rurais.

Embora no seu período de vigência a lei pouco tenha influenciado consumo e costumes —raras bacias têm comitê instituído ou negociado— a redefinição das normas legais sobre recursos hídricos estimulou a organização de interesses que envolvem empresas e Estado.

em alguns lugares as nascentes, córregos e ribeirões secos obrigaram a população a usar a água dos caminhões-pipas das prefeituras, principalmente no Médio Jequitinhonha. Noutros casos, manifesta-se a escassez quando as nascentes perderam muito em volume, obrigando famílias a fazer rodízio para coletar água dos minadouros; em algumas situações só a coletam a cada 3 dias e apenas para parte do consumo doméstico; nesses casos, não há possibilidade de banho e lavagem de roupas todos os dias.
Em sua grande maioria, aquelas são formadas por consumidores diretos, enquanto a população urbana consome água por meio da empresa que a trata e distribui.
Os comitês de bacias hidrográficas não costituíram-se ainda em espaço de debates e produção de acordos

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household and community domestic water access alongside agricultural and watershed water-resource uses in the Jequitinhonha Valley. Although rural inhabitants are primarily characterized as direct consumers of natural springs and streams rather than utility customers, the paper empirically describes household domestic water supply, communal spring-capture piping, reliance on municipal water-tanker trucks (caminhões-pipas), rainwater cisterns (Programa Um Milhão de Cisternas), and relocation to rural villages (povoados) where municipal government assumes water provision.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the literal/plain wording ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper examines customary community water-sharing governance (regulação comunitária / normas costumeiras over spring access and rotation), local municipal patronage, and statutory water-resource governance under Brazil's Law No. 9.433/1997 (ANA, river basin committees, bulk water outorga). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, Criterion 2 is NOT met: (1) Law No. 9.433/1997 and river basin committees regulate bulk river-basin water resources (hydropower, irrigation) rather than household water service access, and the authors explicitly state that in the study period/region the law had barely influenced consumption and basin committees had not yet been constituted as spaces of debate or agreement (unanalysed macro-governance background); (2) the empirical fieldwork examines peasant cultural perceptions of raw water quality ('água fina' vs 'água grande', 'água é dom'), informal neighbour/kinship spring-sharing customs, and cultural reluctance toward rainwater cisterns, rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs/cost recovery, official discretion/accommodation, enforcement of service rules, or utility regulatory structure).
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative empirical field study conducted in 1999-2002 across 22 rural communities and 188 interviewed rural families in six municipalities of the Upper, Middle, and Lower Jequitinhonha Valley, combining semi-structured family interviews with community-wide group discussions.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative household and community water access and availability outcomes under spring depletion and drought, including 3-day collection rationing/rotation (rodízio) at springs, inability to bathe or wash clothes daily, women's increased distance and time burden fetching water, reliance on municipal tanker trucks (caminhões-pipas), low enthusiasm for rainwater cisterns, and drought-related migration to rural villages (povoados).
criterion_notes.c5: Provides sufficient information to identify the population and unit of analysis (188 rural peasant families across 22 rural communities in Minas Gerais), qualitative study design (household interviews and community meetings), empirical focus (peasant cultural perceptions and customary spring-sharing norms under environmental scarcity), and qualitative household water availability/scarcity outcomes, though no formal rule-type service-access exposure is empirically evaluated.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Portuguese, which is directly eligible without translation under Criterion 9.

study_design: Qualitative empirical case study using semi-structured household interviews and community group discussions (1999-2002)
population_and_sample: 188 rural peasant families across 22 rural communities in six municipalities (Turmalina, Veredinha, Medina, Joaíma, Monte Formoso, and Jequitinhonha) of the Upper, Middle, and Lower Jequitinhonha Valley, Minas Gerais, Brazil (units of analysis: rural household/family and rural community).
exposure: Peasant cultural perceptions of water ('água-dom', 'água fina' vs 'água grande') and informal customary community spring-sharing norms under seasonal/environmental scarcity, contrasted conceptually with macro-level river-basin water-resources legislation (Law No. 9.433/1997, ANA, river basin committees).
outcome: Qualitative household and community water access and scarcity practices, including 3-day collection rotation (rodízio) at diminishing springs, reduced domestic water for bathing/laundry and home gardens, women's time/distance burden fetching water, use of municipal water-tanker trucks (caminhões-pipas), reluctance toward rainwater cisterns, and relocation to rural villages (povoados).
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) applying the 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification of Criterion 2. While the qualitative fieldwork (188 rural families in 22 communities in the Jequitinhonha Valley, 1999-2002) describes rural household domestic water scarcity, spring-collection rotation, municipal tanker-truck use, cistern reluctance, and village migration, it does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access. Brazil's Water Law (Law No. 9.433/1997, ANA, river basin committees, bulk water outorga) governs river-basin bulk water resources rather than household service access and is explicitly noted by the authors as having barely influenced local practices in the study period, with river basin committees not yet functioning as spaces of debate or agreement (macro-governance background). Empirically, the study investigates peasant cultural perceptions of natural water quality and informal customary neighbour/kinship sharing of natural springs. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 ('institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), community customary water governance and statutory/municipal governance context would qualify for inclusion.
